evaluated.name: OperatingAssetBuildFundedByShortDebt
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at), 1))), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Receivables and inventory that a firm funds by drawing on short-term debt represent an operating cycle that does not pay for itself; the combination of swelling operating assets and rising revolver balances precedes both inventory write-downs and refinancing stress, whereas the same asset build funded internally is ordinary growth.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly identified that Δdlc appears inside the standard accrual construct, so the gate was partly a transform of the leg it conditioned; restricting the accrual leg to the asset side, Δ(act − che), removes dlc entirely and makes the funding variable a clean, economically exogenous state. The mechanism — who financed the operating cycle — is untested in the archive and distinct from both the static leverage gate and the cash-drain gate, since a firm that borrows short-term can keep its cash balance flat and evade both.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ThreeYearCashBackedProfitGeneration
evaluated.expression: IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(SUB(revt, cogs), 3), SUB(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 3))), at))
evaluated.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings are best measured over a full multi-year stretch: the gross profit a firm has cumulatively earned over three years, less the working capital that expansion permanently consumed, is the profit that was actually available to owners rather than recycled into receivables and inventory.
evaluated.reasoning: The defective cumulative-profit denominator is eliminated — absorption is now expressed as a difference in the numerator with total assets as a uniformly positive deflator — so the sign can no longer flip for the low-profit distressed firms the measure targets. The three-year horizon is the economic point rather than a parameter tweak: it distinguishes firms that generate cash-backed profit through a whole investment cycle from those whose single-year cash conversion is a timing accident, and it restores coverage relative to the five-year version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AbnormalAccrualBeyondSalesNeed
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1))), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm needs additional working capital in proportion to its revenue expansion at its own established operating-cycle intensity; only the accrual *in excess of* that mechanically required amount reflects discretionary recognition, so subtracting the expected build isolates genuine accounting aggressiveness from ordinary growth financing.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has approached this idea only through gates that mute the accrual for growing firms, which discards information rather than adjusting it; here the expected accrual — last year's working-capital intensity multiplied by this year's sales change — is explicitly subtracted, producing a residual that stays informative for high-growth and low-growth firms alike. This is the natural sharpening of the mechanism behind the archive's best signal, and it deflates by assets with a firm-specific expectation model rather than a rank gate, so it should raise the cross-sectional slope and the long-leg quality simultaneously.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildDuringProfitDecline
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers reach for accounting flexibility precisely when the underlying business is deteriorating, so a working-capital build coinciding with falling profitability is the signature of an attempt to mask decline, whereas the same build at a firm with improving profitability reflects an expanding, healthy operating base.
evaluated.reasoning: Profitability *change* has been tested only as an additive leg, where it delivered a weak 2.9% alpha because it discarded the profitability anchor; as a conditioning state it plays a different role, identifying the population in which accrual manipulation has motive. It is economically distinct from the demand gate — a firm can grow revenue while its margins collapse, which is exactly the discount-and-stuff pattern this gate targets and the sales-growth gate misses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AbnormalAccrualConservatismStreak
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1)))), 0), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Reporting conservatism is a durable managerial regime rather than an annual outcome, and the cleanest evidence of it is a repeated record of working-capital builds falling short of what revenue growth would have justified; five years of such restraint identifies management that does not use the operating cycle to manufacture reported performance.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's streak signal produced the highest alpha t-stat on record (5.98) but a poor 0.206 Sharpe, and its diagnosed weaknesses were a raw-accrual criterion contaminated by growth and a weak sales-deflated margin anchor; counting years of *abnormal* accrual restraint fixes the criterion, and pairing it with the industry-relative profitability anchor that carries the archive's alpha should fix the portfolio instability. This tests whether the persistence dimension, once measured on the correct variable, adds information beyond the current year's accrual state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalFundedByTermDebt
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(dltt, 1), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-term borrowing is meant to fund long-lived assets; a firm issuing term debt while its receivables and inventory swell is capitalizing an operating-cycle problem into its balance sheet, which both confirms that the accrual was not self-funded and locks in fixed charges against earnings that will not materialize.
evaluated.reasoning: The short-term-debt version of this idea was correctly criticized because Δdlc sits inside the accrual construct, forcing a weakened asset-side accrual leg that cut alpha to 2.3%; long-term debt appears nowhere in the working-capital measure, so the gate is a clean state variable and the full, proven accrual leg can be retained. It is also distinct from the static leverage gate, which measures the level of indebtedness rather than the act of raising new external financing in the same year as the accrual.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildWithCostOverhang
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(SUB(GROWTH(cogs, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm's cost of goods grows faster than its revenue, its cost base has become rigid relative to demand; a working-capital build in that state is inventory and receivables produced at costs the market will not reimburse, so the eventual markdown falls straight through to earnings rather than being absorbed by margin.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces a genuinely new conditioning state — cost-side rigidity, measured as the wedge between cost growth and revenue growth — that no archive signal has used, and it is economically distinct from both the demand gate (which sees only the revenue side) and the profitability-decline gate (which sees the net outcome rather than its cost-structure cause). It also differs from the accepted OverproductionVsCostBase signal, which compares asset growth to costs as an additive leg; here costs versus sales define the state in which the accrual is dangerous, not the accrual measure itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildWithThinCashBuffer
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The consequence of a working-capital build depends on the liquidity stock available to carry it: a cash-rich firm can hold slow-moving inventory and stretched receivables until they convert at full value, while a cash-poor firm must discount, factor, or write them down, converting an accounting distortion into a realized loss.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the rejected horizon tweak with a new state variable — the *stock* of liquidity rather than its flow — which is economically distinct from the cash-drain gate (a firm can be drawing down a large buffer harmlessly, or holding a tiny balance flat and be one shock from distress) and from static leverage, which measures claims rather than the reserves available to meet them. It uses the cash level, not its change, so it is not a re-expression of the accrual leg through the cash-flow identity, and it targets precisely the population where accrual reversal becomes a realized economic loss rather than a reporting adjustment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildUnderDemandUncertainty
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(VOL(GROWTH(sale, 1), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory and receivables committed against an unpredictable revenue stream are far more likely to become obsolete or uncollectible than the same commitment at a firm with stable demand; it is the *variance* of demand, not its current level, that determines whether a working-capital build converts at book value.
evaluated.reasoning: Every state variable tested so far is a first moment — the level or change of sales, cash, debt, or margin — whereas forecast risk about future demand is what actually governs write-down probability, and it is nearly uncorrelated with contemporaneous growth. This also revives the earnings-stability dimension that failed as an additive leg (alpha 2.7%) by using it in the role where the archive shows volatility-type variables belong: as a conditioning state on the accrual rather than as a return-predictive characteristic on its own.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildOutOfCharacter
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: At a firm with a historically stable margin structure, a sudden working-capital build is out of character and therefore informative about deliberate accounting or operational stress; at a firm whose margins swing routinely, the same build is within the normal range of business noise and carries little signal.
evaluated.reasoning: This inverts the conditioning logic of the archive's gates, which all amplify the accrual in *distressed* states, by proposing instead that the accrual is most informative where the firm's own reporting baseline is most predictable — a signal-to-noise argument rather than a liquidation-risk argument. Running it alongside Signal 2, which gates on high demand volatility, makes the batch decisive about whether accrual information is amplified by risk or by baseline stability, a question no single-gate test can settle.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualPerAbsorptiveCapacity
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), ADD(che, SUB(revt, cogs))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What determines whether a working-capital build becomes an earnings event is the firm's capacity to absorb its reversal, and that capacity is the sum of the liquid reserves it holds and the annual gross profit it generates; the same dollar build is trivial against a large absorptive base and existential against a small one.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the stacked-modifier construction the critic rejected and replaces the universal total-assets deflator — used by every one of the archive's thirty-plus accrual legs — with an economically motivated capacity denominator that fuses a quality quantity (gross profit) with a liquidity quantity (cash), so the interaction is structural rather than a rank product. The denominator is a sum of two almost always positive quantities, which avoids the small-and-sign-flipping problem that killed the earlier per-gross-profit ratio, and total assets, which mostly proxies for capital intensity, is removed from the scaling entirely.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IncrementalProfitConversion
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth in reported gross profit is durable only when it is not matched dollar-for-dollar by growth in the operating cycle; when working capital expands faster than the profit increment it supposedly supports, the incremental profit exists only on paper and will not repeat.
evaluated.reasoning: I abandon the non-current accrual residual, which the critic correctly showed would be dominated by depreciation and would merely proxy for capital intensity while sacrificing coverage through oancf. This construction instead benchmarks the accrual against the *profit increment* rather than against revenue, assets, or a sales-growth expectation — a comparison no archive signal makes — and it directly operationalizes the task's distinction between durable cash earnings and accounting noise at the margin where earnings growth is generated.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NoCreditForDeclineDrivenShedding
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(MAX(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1))), at), MUL(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1))), at), INDICATOR(DELTA(sale, 1), 0))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Abnormal accrual builds should always be penalized, but abnormal accrual *releases* should be credited only when revenue is growing; a shrinking firm that sheds receivables and inventory is liquidating, not converting, and its negative residual is a symptom of decline rather than evidence of cash-backed performance.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly identified that simply switching off the expectation term inverts the intended economics, so the asymmetry is now imposed where it belongs — on the residual itself: when sales grow the indicator equals one and the MAX returns the full symmetric residual, while when sales fall the MAX floors the residual at zero, preserving every penalty but removing the reward for decline-driven shedding. This is a one-sided treatment of the *residual*, not of the raw accrual, so it is not the degenerate build-indicator variant already shown to reproduce the ungated result.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualPenaltyWhereArbitrageIsCostly
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(LOG(at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual mispricing persists only where correcting it is costly: at small, thinly followed firms the accounting distortion is not arbitraged away, whereas at large firms analyst scrutiny and institutional trading impound the accrual information into prices quickly, so the accrual leg should be amplified where information processing is weakest.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the confounded anchor-purification test — where the accrual entered both legs with the same sign — with the one class of conditioning variable the archive has never examined: limits to arbitrage rather than firm fundamentals. It is a falsifiable claim about *why* the anomaly survives rather than about which firms are economically fragile, and because FF5 already prices the size factor, a surviving alpha would show the amplification is informational rather than a mechanical small-cap tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ThreeYearIncrementalConversion
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 3)), SUB(SUB(revt, cogs), LAG(SUB(revt, cogs), 3))), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings are a multi-year property: a firm that has grown its gross profit over three years while holding its operating cycle flat has structurally improved conversion, whereas a one-year favorable comparison can be produced by a single quarter of receivable collection timing.
evaluated.reasoning: The one-year increment comparison generated the archive's best alpha, and the open question is whether the effect reflects transitory timing that reverses quickly or a durable regime — the horizon test settles it and speaks directly to the task's distinction between durable cash earnings and accounting noise. Unlike the earlier five-year cumulative construct that lost coverage (0.079), a three-year lag on well-populated balance-sheet and income-statement items should retain roughly 0.10 coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IncrementalConversionAgainstBottomLine
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(ni, 1)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The profit that must fund the operating cycle is the bottom line, not the gross line: gross profit ignores overhead, interest and taxes that also consume cash, so the increment in net income is the economically correct benchmark for judging whether a working-capital build was affordable.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the single most consequential measurement choice inside the archive's best signal — which profit increment is the right yardstick — and the answer is not settled a priori, since gross profit is less manipulable while net income is what actually finances working capital. Running it against Signal 1 on identical construction tells the final generation whether to build on a top-line or bottom-line benchmark, a question no anchor-deflator experiment in this archive has addressed because those all concerned the *level* leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RepeatedIncrementalConversion
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1), DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1)), 0), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A management team that repeatedly grows profit faster than it grows receivables and inventory is running a structurally cash-generative model; counting how many of the past five years show this pattern identifies a durable operating discipline rather than a favorable single-year comparison.
evaluated.reasoning: Persistence counts have twice produced the archive's highest alpha t-statistics (5.98 for the raw streak, 6.03 for the increment leg) but the raw streak used a growth-contaminated criterion; applying the count to the increment comparison combines the archive's two best-performing ideas at the level of the *criterion* rather than by stacking modifiers. Discreteness is the known risk to Sharpe, which the continuous industry-relative profitability anchor is there to mitigate by breaking ties within each count bucket.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ConversionRegimeDeterioration
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Each firm has a characteristic rate at which profit growth requires working-capital investment, set by its customers, credit terms and production technology; what signals emerging accounting stress is a deterioration relative to that firm's own established conversion norm, not the level of the gap.
evaluated.reasoning: This addresses the same economic problem the rejected industry z-score wrapper aimed at — business-model differences in required working capital — but with a firm-level rather than sector-level benchmark, which is strictly finer since conversion technology varies enormously within any industry classification, and it retains winsorization so outlier control is not sacrificed. It is a change of benchmark, not of normalization: the signal now measures a within-firm regime shift in cash conversion, a state variable no archive entry constructs on the increment gap.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginalProfitPerOperatingCapital
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1), ADD(che, ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful measure of earnings quality at the margin is how much additional gross profit a firm generates per dollar of operating capital it has tied up in cash, receivables and inventory; a high marginal return on that base means growth is being produced without accumulating soft assets.
evaluated.reasoning: I drop the additive ablation, which the critic rightly judged to be a three-way stack of published effects, and replace it with a genuine ratio interaction in which the quality theme supplies the numerator (the profit increment) and the accruals theme supplies the denominator (the operating capital stock the firm must carry), a construction absent from the entire archive, whose accrual legs are all differences or rank gates. Including the cash balance in the denominator keeps it positive for the overwhelming majority of firms, avoiding the sign-flip defect that disqualified the earlier per-gross-profit ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkIncrementalConversion
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings require a profitable franchise *and* profit growth that is not absorbed by the operating cycle, and the two cannot compensate for one another: a firm should be scored by whichever dimension is weaker, because either failure alone makes reported performance unreliable.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the saturated gating template entirely — no rank multiplier, no state variable — and instead applies the non-compensatory MIN rule to the archive's best-performing accrual leg, a pairing never tested since the earlier weakest-link used the raw level accrual and still reached 4.5% alpha with a 0.372 Sharpe. Because the conjunctive rule concentrates the long leg on firms that are simultaneously profitable and cash-converting, it is the natural final-round test of whether the increment mechanism's 6.0% alpha can be sharpened by refusing to let strong profitability offset weak conversion.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorstYearConversionShortfall
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(TS_MAX(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm's willingness to let the operating cycle swallow its profit growth is revealed by its worst year, not its average: one episode of severe conversion failure in five years marks a management team that will do it again, and that latent tendency contaminates today's reported earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: The tail-statistic idea earned only 3.8% alpha when applied to the raw accrual, but the raw accrual conflates growth financing with conversion failure, whereas the profit-benchmarked gap isolates the behaviour the hypothesis describes — so this is a re-test of a temporal statistic on a materially better-measured variable. It also complements the streak count already evaluated, since a count measures frequency while a maximum measures severity, and the two can diverge sharply for firms with one catastrophic year.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BothLinesConversionConsensus
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MIN(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 1)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(ni, 1)), at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profit growth is credibly cash-backed only when it outpaces the working-capital build on both the gross line, which is hard to manipulate but ignores overhead, and the bottom line, which captures all cash claims but is itself accrual-laden; requiring agreement between the two benchmarks screens out firms whose favorable comparison is an artifact of which profit measure is used.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive tested both benchmarks separately — gross gave the highest alpha (6.0%) while net gave a higher slope (fmb 5.36, alpha 4.8%) — which is exactly the pattern that motivates a consensus rule rather than a choice between them, since each corrects a different weakness of the other. The MIN is applied across two measurements of the same economic quantity, not across themes, so it is a robustness restriction on the accrual leg rather than a re-run of the weakest-link architecture.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IntensitySpaceConversionGap
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale), 1), DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings quality improves when a firm needs less working capital per dollar of revenue while earning more margin per dollar of revenue; expressing both the accrual and the profit change in intensity space makes the comparison scale-free and directly measures whether the business model is becoming more or less cash-generative.
evaluated.reasoning: This attacks the family's fmb weakness from a different direction than Signal 1: rather than changing the deflator of a dollar difference, it moves the entire comparison into per-revenue intensities, which removes firm size and asset intensity from both terms simultaneously and yields a bounded, well-behaved cross-sectional distribution. The standalone intensity drift measure reached only 2.4% alpha without a profit benchmark or a quality anchor, so this tests whether that construct's weakness was its scaling or its missing margin comparison.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DoublyVerifiedProfitConversion
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MIN(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 1)), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profit growth is genuinely cash-backed only if it passes two independent checks — it was not absorbed by an expanding operating cycle, and it left a visible trace in the cash balance; a firm that satisfies the first but not the second has merely relocated the shortfall from working capital into some other use of funds.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the deflator swap the critic correctly judged to be both cosmetic and technically backwards, and instead adds a second, independent verification channel: the cash balance change, which the archive has only ever used as a multiplicative gate, never as a co-equal condition. The conjunctive MIN rule is the aggregation the archive validated this generation (Sharpe 0.439, fmb 4.90), and applying it across two verification tests of the same profit increment is a new economic claim about corroboration rather than a crossing of two existing signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ConversionWithGenuineProfitGrowth
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MIN(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1)), at), 1)), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A favorable conversion gap has two very different sources — profit growing faster than the operating cycle, or the operating cycle collapsing faster than profit — and only the first is evidence of durable cash earnings; requiring genuine profit growth alongside the favorable gap excludes firms that merely liquidated working capital while their business shrank.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the economics that the expectation-model family tried and failed to capture (abnormal accrual 3.8%, decline-shedding correction 4.3%), reimplemented through the conjunctive rule that actually worked in this archive rather than through a modeled expected accrual. It avoids the flagged horizon crossing entirely, keeps full coverage at 0.112 rather than paying the three-year lag's 0.093, and makes a falsifiable claim: if the leader's alpha survives this restriction, its long leg is genuinely growing firms, and if it collapses, the effect was liquidation-driven all along.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualBuildInDaysOfCost
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), cogs), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Receivables and inventory are carried at cost, so the natural unit for a working-capital build is days of the annual cost base it represents; a firm adding many days of cost to its operating cycle is funding goods and credit its throughput does not support, regardless of how large its asset base happens to be.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly identified that differencing against cost *growth* perversely rewards firms with exploding costs; expressing the build relative to the cost *level* removes that inversion entirely and states the measure in the operational unit accountants actually use. Cost of goods sold is large, strictly positive and far more stable than gross profit or an operating-capital base, so this deflator should also compress the heavy tails responsible for the increment family's weak cross-sectional slope while remaining economically distinct from the asset, sales and absorptive-capacity scalings already tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: CashBackedPersistenceScore
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)), TREND(RATIO(ib, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose reported earnings are cash-backed (low total accruals) AND whose profitability is both stable and improving have durable, repeatable earnings that the market under-extrapolates, while high-accrual/noisy-earnings firms mean-revert.
considered.reasoning: The accrual channel measures how much of reported income is non-cash, while low ROA volatility plus a positive ROA trend measures whether the earnings level is a persistent state rather than a transitory print. Combining all three ranks isolates firms where low accruals genuinely signal durable cash performance instead of merely a low-growth or shrinking balance sheet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashEarningsInformationRatio
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ib), at), 3), VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Persistent cash-flow-over-earnings surplus is informative only relative to the noise in the firm's earnings process; scaling the smoothed accrual surplus by earnings volatility yields an accounting signal-to-noise ratio that predicts returns.
considered.reasoning: A three-year average of (cash flow minus income) captures a durable conservative-accrual state rather than a one-year timing artifact, and dividing by ROA volatility converts it into a per-unit-of-noise measure. Firms with a large, stable cash surplus relative to earnings noise have genuinely cash-backed performance, whereas the same surplus in a volatile firm is uninformative.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IndustryWCAccrualGrossProfit
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Within an industry, firms that grow gross profitability without inflating working capital convert operating strength into cash, while peers with similar margins but rising working-capital accruals are financing reported profit with receivables and inventory.
considered.reasoning: Balance-sheet working-capital accruals isolate the most manipulable component of income, and gross profitability is the cleanest, least-manipulated quality measure; both are heavily industry-dependent, so industry z-scoring makes the interaction comparable across business models. The joint rank targets cash-validated profitability rather than either effect alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualTiltedByProfitTrend
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1))), RANK(TREND(RATIO(ib, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: The low-accrual premium is stronger among firms whose profitability is on an improving multi-year path, because there low accruals reflect genuine cash conversion of a rising earnings stream rather than balance-sheet shrinkage; the accrual effect should therefore be continuously amplified by profitability trend, not switched on and off.
considered.reasoning: The hard 0/1 gate is replaced by a continuous gate, RANK(TREND(ROA,5)) in [0,1], multiplying a signed, winsorized accrual z-score, so trend-negative firms receive a damped rather than annihilated accrual tilt and never pile up at an artificial zero. Adding the raw accrual rank as a second SUMRANK channel preserves the unconditional low-accrual main effect, keeping the composite monotone in accruals while letting the interaction term steepen the slope in the high-quality region.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ConservativeAccrualStreakMargin
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(oancf, ib), 0), 5), TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Repeated years in which operating cash flow exceeds reported income indicate a conservative, habitual reporting regime rather than a one-year timing artifact; when this streak coincides with an improving gross margin, the firm is converting genuinely widening operating profitability into cash and future earnings are durable.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the accrual-volatility (Dechow-Dichev) construct entirely and instead uses a reporting-persistence count — how many of the last five years had cash flow above income — which measures the habitual conservatism of the accounting policy rather than the noise in accrual estimation. Pairing it with the five-year trend in gross margin (the least manipulable profitability line) tests whether the cash surplus accompanies real operating improvement, so it is neither a standard quality score nor a duplicate of the level-based accrual signals in the batch.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualSurpriseNoiseWeighted
considered.expression: NEG(MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 5)), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(ni, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: What predicts reversal is the innovation in accruals relative to the firm's own normal accrual level, and this innovation is least verifiable — hence most likely to be opportunistic and most likely to reverse — when the firm's earnings process is already noisy.
considered.reasoning: The degenerate NEG(product of two non-negative ranks) is replaced by a signed, naturally zero-centered accrual surprise (current accruals minus their own five-year mean), multiplied by a noise weight in [0,1], so the extreme long and short tails are populated only by firms with large negative or positive accrual innovations in noisy-earnings environments, exactly as the hypothesis states. Low-earnings-volatility firms are correctly shrunk toward the neutral middle instead of being pushed to the top, so the signal cannot collapse into a low-volatility quality proxy, and firm-mean differencing removes stable firm-level accrual scale that contaminates purely cross-sectional accrual measures.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OperatingCycleAccrualMarginTrend
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(recch, ADD(invch, apalch)), at), TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: The receivable, inventory and payable components of the cash flow statement are the most discretionary and least verifiable part of accruals; firms that release cash from the operating cycle while their gross margin is genuinely trending upward are converting real competitive improvement into cash, unlike firms whose margin gains sit in receivables and inventory.
considered.reasoning: Cash-flow-statement components (recch, invch, apalch enter oancf with a positive-equals-cash-inflow convention) isolate the operating cycle directly rather than inferring it from noisy balance-sheet differences that are contaminated by mergers and reclassifications. Pairing this with a five-year gross-margin trend separates durable pricing/cost improvement from margin that was manufactured through channel stuffing or inventory build.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ConservativeAccrualStreakMargin
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1)), 0), 5), MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 3))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of negative accruals can be a timing artifact, but a multi-year streak of shrinking non-cash working capital reveals a habitual conservative reporting and tight operating-capital regime; combined with a high sustained gross margin, this identifies firms whose profitability is structurally cash-generating.
considered.reasoning: Counting how many of the last five years had negative working-capital accruals converts a noisy annual flow into a persistence state, which is the concept the economic story actually requires and which no level-based accrual measure captures. The margin leg ensures the streak reflects disciplined cash conversion of a profitable business rather than a firm liquidating working capital while its economics deteriorate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalIntensityDrift
considered.expression: NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale), 1), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not the dollar accrual but whether non-cash working capital is expanding faster than the revenue base that justifies it; a rising working-capital-per-dollar-of-sales ratio means receivables and inventory are being built without commensurate demand, and that gap reverses into future earnings and returns.
considered.reasoning: Benchmarking the accrual stock against contemporaneous revenue makes this a revenue-conditioned accrual measure rather than the asset-deflated Sloan variable, so a firm can have large positive accruals and still score well if sales grew proportionally — the ranking is not a monotone re-parameterization of total accruals. Sales is almost always strictly positive, so the deflator is numerically stable, and I have dropped the earnings-stability gate entirely because the critic is right that the accrual anomaly is not concentrated in low-volatility firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DepreciationConservatismProfitability
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dpc, sale)), MA(RATIO(ni, ceq), 3))
considered.hypothesis: Depreciation is the largest non-discretionary-looking but in fact highly discretionary accrual; within an industry, firms charging more depreciation per dollar of sales are reporting conservatively, so when such a firm still shows high sustained ROE its cash earnings power is understated rather than inflated.
considered.reasoning: I abandoned the taxes-payable channel because the critic is correct that Δtxp is a current-liability increase that mechanically *reduces* accruals — the sign in my original was backwards — and because txp is sparsely populated and economically trivial relative to assets. The depreciation-policy channel keeps the same "is reported profit validated by conservative accounting?" mechanism using dpc, which is well populated on the cash flow statement, and industry z-scoring removes the capital-intensity confound so the leg measures policy conservatism rather than asset mix.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualPenaltyAtLowProfitability
considered.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))))
considered.hypothesis: A given working-capital build is far more dangerous for a firm with a thin profit base, which cannot absorb the eventual write-down, than for a highly profitable firm whose cash generation easily covers it; the accrual penalty should therefore steepen as sustained gross profitability falls.
considered.reasoning: The unstable gross-profit denominator is replaced by a bounded [0,1] gate, RANK(NEG(smoothed gross profitability)), multiplying an asset-deflated, winsorized accrual z-score, so there is no sign flip or explosion when gross profit is small or negative — the structural defect the critic identified is removed while the economic claim survives intact. The first SUMRANK channel retains the gross-profitability main effect so that high-quality firms are not shrunk into the neutral middle by the gate, giving a monotone quality tilt plus a quality-conditional accrual slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RetainedEarningsCashGap
considered.expression: NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), at), RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Retained earnings growth records what management says it earned and kept; the change in the cash balance records what actually arrived. When retained earnings rise year after year without any corresponding cash accumulation, the reported profit was absorbed by soft accruals and unproductive investment, and subsequent returns are poor.
considered.reasoning: This drops the leverage leg the critic correctly identified as the net-debt-issuance anomaly and replaces it with a direct book-versus-cash reconciliation that no financing or accrual factor in the archive measures: it compares the stock of claimed cumulative profit to the stock of realized cash. Both legs are deflated by total assets rather than by book equity, so negative or near-zero equity cannot generate sign-flipped extremes, and the winsorization only trims genuine outliers rather than repairing a structural defect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualWithEarningsStability
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))), NEG(VOL(RATIO(ni, ceq), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: The task's core story is that low accruals plus stable earnings identify genuinely cash-backed performance; stable ROE means the earnings level is a persistent state, so a low accrual attached to it is credible evidence of repeatable cash generation rather than a transitory swing in the operating cycle.
considered.reasoning: Every strong archive result so far uses gross profitability as the quality leg, leaving the literal earnings-persistence dimension untested against the industry-neutralized accrual leg — this fills that gap and tells us whether the quality channel that matters is profit *level* or profit *stability*. The five-year ROE volatility window will reduce coverage somewhat, which is the diagnostic cost of the test and is why I run it alongside, not instead of, the profitability-leg variants.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualPenaltyAtHighLeverage
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual build must eventually be financed; a highly levered firm cannot carry an inflating receivable and inventory position without a funding or covenant problem, so the reversal of accruals is faster and more damaging when the balance sheet is already stretched.
considered.reasoning: The prior conditional signal (accrual penalty amplified at low profitability) delivered fmb 4.53 and 5.2% alpha, so the conditional architecture works; this changes the conditioning variable to leverage, which is nearly orthogonal to gross margin and captures the financing-capacity mechanism instead of the profit-cushion mechanism. The gate is a bounded [0,1] rank and the accrual leg is asset-deflated and winsorized, so there are no denominator sign flips, and the gross-profitability main effect is retained in the first channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WeakestLinkCashQuality
considered.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings require both conditions simultaneously — real operating profitability and no accrual inflation — so a firm should be judged by its weaker dimension: high margins financed by a receivable build are not cash-backed, and clean accruals at a firm with no gross profit are not earnings at all.
considered.reasoning: Taking the minimum of two industry-standardized legs is a conjunctive, non-additive operator: unlike SUMRANK or the numerator subtraction of cash-based operating profitability, it refuses to let a strong profitability score compensate for an aggressive accrual, which is exactly the economic claim the task makes and is not what any published cash-profitability measure computes. It uses the same well-covered balance-sheet inputs as the archive leader, so any difference in performance is attributable purely to the conjunctive versus compensatory aggregation rule.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalBloatVsPeers
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The informative quantity is the accumulated stock of non-cash working capital a firm carries per dollar of sales relative to its industry peers, not this year's flow: persistent bloat means receivables and inventory that peers with the same business model do not need, which eventually becomes write-offs and margin pressure.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the smoothing-horizon tweak the critic rejected and switches from a flow to a stock construct, which is a different economic mechanism: balance-sheet bloat and stale operating assets rather than the annual accrual that must reverse next year. Deflating by sales and industry-standardizing makes the level comparable across operating cycles, and pairing it with industry-relative gross profitability asks whether the bloat is being carried by a genuinely profitable franchise or is masking deteriorating economics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualInnovationVsOwnRegime
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), MA(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 5)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms have permanently different normal accrual levels because of their operating cycle, so the reversal-prone quantity is the deviation of this year's accrual from the firm's own multi-year norm; a profitable firm whose accruals suddenly jump above its own regime is the clearest manipulation candidate.
considered.reasoning: The critic is right that TS_RANK over five annual points yields at most five values and reproduces the lumpy-tie problem, so the firm-relative concept is now implemented as a continuous demeaning — current accrual minus its own five-year moving average — which preserves the within-firm interpretation with no ties at all. Winsorization controls the innovation tail, and the industry-relative gross-profitability leg supplies the quality dimension that distinguishes an accrual jump at a healthy franchise from routine noise at a marginal firm.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AsymmetricAccrualBuildPenalty
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1), INDICATOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 0))))
considered.hypothesis: The accrual anomaly is asymmetric: positive accruals are discretionary builds of receivables and inventory that must reverse, while negative accruals often reflect distress-driven liquidation of working capital rather than superior cash conversion, so only the build side should be penalized.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the redundant level-plus-change construction with a genuine functional-form test — whether the accrual-return relation is one-sided — which no signal in the archive has examined and which speaks directly to distinguishing cash-backed performance from forced deleveraging. Firms with negative accruals receive zero in the penalty leg, but the continuous industry-relative gross-profitability leg breaks those ties, so the sort stays smooth and the portfolio composition stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildWithoutDemand
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: A working-capital build is benign when it funds genuine revenue expansion — a growing firm must carry more receivables and inventory — but malignant when sales are flat or falling, because then it reflects unsold inventory, channel stuffing, or receivables the firm cannot collect.
considered.reasoning: Both prior conditional gates (low profitability, high leverage) delivered fmb above 4.5, so the architecture is validated; this substitutes demand growth as the gate, which is the economically correct scaler for working capital and is close to orthogonal to both the profit cushion and the balance-sheet constraint already tested. It should sharpen the short leg specifically by separating growth-driven accruals from stagnation-driven accruals, a distinction no archive signal makes.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildWithMarginErosion
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))), DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Rising working capital combined with a deteriorating gross margin is the classic manipulation pattern — the firm is buying revenue with looser credit terms and discounting while capitalizing the cost in inventory — whereas a lean balance sheet with widening margins reflects real pricing power converted to cash.
considered.reasoning: Every strong archive result uses the *level* of profitability as the quality leg, so the direction of profitability has never been tested against the accrual leg; margin change is nearly orthogonal to margin level and captures the deterioration that makes an accrual build dangerous. Using a one-year margin change on well-covered income-statement items avoids the coverage collapse that destroyed the five-year cash-flow-statement trend signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualWithRetainedProfitHistory
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(re, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Retained earnings relative to assets is the cumulative record of profits a firm has actually earned and kept over its whole life, an inherently persistent quality measure; a clean current accrual attached to a long history of retained profit identifies established cash generators, whereas clean accruals at a firm with a depleted retained-earnings base reflect a fragile, unproven business.
considered.reasoning: The quality leg in this archive has only ever been contemporaneous profitability or short-window earnings volatility, both of which are one- to five-year measures; retained earnings capture profit persistence over decades and are known to relate to firm maturity and payout capacity, giving a genuinely different quality dimension to interact with the accrual. It also uses only well-populated fields, so coverage should be at least as high as the 0.121–0.130 range seen for the re- and che-based signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalSlackVsOwnBest
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale), TS_MIN(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale), 5))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Every firm has demonstrated, at some point in the recent past, how leanly it can run its operating cycle; the gap between today's working capital per dollar of sales and that self-demonstrated minimum measures accumulated operating slack — uncollected receivables and unsold inventory the firm has proven it does not need — and that slack must eventually be written down.
considered.reasoning: This is neither the archived flow accrual nor the archived peer-relative bloat level: the benchmark is the firm's own five-year best operating efficiency, so permanent business-model differences in working-capital intensity are differenced out without imposing an industry classification, and a firm can look bloated versus peers yet clean versus its own attainable frontier. The distance-from-own-extreme construction is continuous, avoiding the tie problem of the streak signal, and pairing it with industry-relative gross profitability asks whether the slack sits at a franchise strong enough to absorb the write-down.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualPenaltyAtHighProfitability
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))))
considered.hypothesis: Mispricing from accruals is largest exactly where investors have the most reason to extrapolate — highly profitable firms whose visible margins the market capitalizes eagerly; when such a firm's profit is not cash-backed, the disappointment is severe, whereas low-profit firms are already priced for bad news so their accruals carry less surprise.
considered.reasoning: The archive's low-profitability gate (fmb 4.53, alpha 5.2%) assumed the accrual penalty is largest where the profit cushion is thin; this proposal reverses the conditioning direction on identical inputs, so the pair jointly identifies which side of the profitability distribution the accrual anomaly actually lives on — a substantive economic question, not a re-blend of archived legs. It abandons the MIN aggregation the critic correctly judged exhausted and keeps a continuous bounded gate plus the profitability main effect so the sort stays smooth.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierStretchAsNegativeQuality
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, wcap), dlc), 1), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Standard accrual measures treat a build in non-debt current liabilities as a good thing because it mechanically reduces accruals, but a ballooning payables balance is usually a firm financing itself by stretching suppliers under liquidity pressure, so the liability side should enter with the opposite sign from the Sloan convention.
considered.reasoning: Rather than deleting the liability term as the critic rightly called a minimal edit, this flips its sign and tests it as a standalone quality channel against industry-relative profitability: the claim is that payables growth is a distress and supplier-financing signal, not an earnings-quality improvement. Because every archive accrual leg nets this term in with a positive earnings-quality interpretation, a positive result here would imply that all existing composites are mixing two opposite-signed economic forces inside one variable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorstYearAccrualAggression
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(TS_MAX(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 5)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Accounting aggressiveness is a management trait revealed at its extreme, not on average: a firm that has posted one enormous working-capital build in the last five years has demonstrated a willingness to inflate reported performance, and that latent tendency contaminates its current earnings even in a year when accruals look clean.
considered.reasoning: Every temporal accrual construct in the archive uses a central tendency — one-year flow, five-year mean deviation, moving average, or a streak count — so the tail of the firm's own accrual distribution is untested, and it is precisely the tail that identifies discretionary reporting behavior versus routine operating-cycle variation. The measure is continuous (unlike the streak, whose Sharpe was 0.206) and pairs with the proven gross-profitability anchor, so a strong result would establish accounting-behavior extremity as a new state variable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildDrainingCash
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1), RANK(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), at))))))
considered.hypothesis: A working-capital build funded out of a shrinking cash balance is qualitatively different from one accompanied by rising cash: the first means reported profit is being consumed by the operating cycle and liquidity is deteriorating, the second means the firm is generating enough cash to fund growth and still accumulate reserves.
considered.reasoning: The gates tested so far are balance-sheet stocks (leverage) or income-statement flows (sales growth, margin); the direction of the cash balance is a distinct, directly observable verification of whether accruals were actually financed internally, and it is the one variable that adjudicates the task's central question of cash-backed versus paper performance. Unlike the failed retained-earnings-versus-cash gap, cash change enters here only as a bounded conditioning rank on the accrual, so it cannot invert the sort the way that standalone difference did.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitFloorWithCleanAccruals
considered.expression: SUMRANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Durable earnings power is best measured by the worst year a firm has endured: a five-year minimum of gross profitability is the floor the business defends through downturns, and clean accruals attached to a high floor identify performance that is both cash-backed and cyclically robust.
considered.reasoning: The archive tested profitability as a level (strong) and as five-year ROE volatility (weak, alpha 2.7%), but never as a downside floor, which is the concept the "persistent, stable earnings" story actually requires and which discards the upside variation that makes a volatility measure penalize good firms. It is continuous, uses the same well-covered income-statement inputs, and if it outperforms the plain level anchor it redirects the remaining generations toward downside-persistence quality rather than contemporaneous profitability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CumulativeProfitAbsorbedByWorkingCapital
considered.expression: NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 5)), TS_SUM(SUB(revt, cogs), 5)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Over a full business cycle, the fraction of cumulative gross profit that has been swallowed by an expanding operating cycle measures how much of a firm's reported profitability was never available as cash; a firm that consumed most of five years of gross profit financing receivables and inventory has been reporting profit it never collected.
considered.reasoning: This is not a concatenation of archived legs: accruals and profitability enter as a single economic quantity — cumulative working-capital expansion expressed as a share of cumulative gross profit — so the interaction is imposed by the accounting identity rather than by averaging two ranks. The denominator is a five-year sum of gross profit, which is large and almost always positive, curing the small-and-sign-flipping denominator problem that sank the earlier per-gross-profit ratio, and the five-year horizon distinguishes structural cash absorption from a single year's timing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CapitalEfficiencyWithCleanAccruals
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(sale, at)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The DuPont decomposition splits profitability into margin and asset turnover, and it is turnover — the speed at which a firm converts its asset base into revenue — that is economically inseparable from accrual quality, because a fast-turning firm collects and sells before it must fund the operating cycle, whereas a slow-turning firm's reported profits are structurally locked up in working capital.
considered.reasoning: Every archive composite has anchored on the margin branch of DuPont, so the turnover branch is an untested and economically prior quality dimension: it speaks directly to whether reported earnings can be converted to cash, which is the task's question, rather than to how much profit is earned per sale. Because turnover and gross profitability are close to negatively correlated across industries, industry standardization is essential and included, and a strong result here would show the accrual effect certifies operating speed rather than pricing power.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RepeatedAccrualBuildPenalty
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1), INDICATOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 0))))
considered.hypothesis: A single year's working-capital build is usually operating noise that reverses on its own, but a build that follows another build is a ratchet — receivables and inventory that failed to convert last year and were added to again — and it is this repeated, unreversed accumulation that predicts write-downs and earnings disappointment.
considered.reasoning: The archived asymmetric penalty conditions only on the contemporaneous sign of the accrual, so the dynamic question of whether accruals reverse or ratchet across years is untested, and it is exactly the distinction between transitory accounting noise and durable balance-sheet deterioration that the task asks us to make. The conditioning term uses the prior-period asset base to detect whether the accrual was also positive a year earlier, the penalty magnitude stays continuous and winsorized, and the gross-profitability anchor breaks ties among the firms whose penalty term is switched off.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildWhileLosingShare
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
considered.hypothesis: What makes an accrual build suspicious is not slow growth per se but slow growth *relative to the firm's industry*: a firm whose revenue lags its peers while its receivables and inventory swell is losing share and propping up reported sales with credit terms and channel stuffing, whereas slow growth in a cyclically depressed industry is shared adversity, not manipulation.
considered.reasoning: The absolute-growth gate produced the archive's best alpha but conflates industry cycles with firm-specific deterioration, so a substantial share of its short leg is simply firms in slow industries; industry-standardizing the gate isolates competitive decline, which is the economic force the mechanism actually claims. If this raises fmb and alpha together, it establishes that the gate works through firm-specific demand failure rather than through an implicit cyclical-industry tilt — a genuine attribution result, not a rescaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildOnAlreadyLongCycle
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), sale))))
considered.hypothesis: A given increment of working capital is far more likely to be uncollectible or obsolete at a firm that already carries a long operating cycle, because such a firm has demonstrated it cannot convert inventory and receivables quickly; adding to an already slow cycle compounds conversion risk, while the same build at a fast-turning firm clears within months.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested the working-capital stock only as an additive leg (Sharpe 0.409); using it instead as the conditioning state for the flow makes an economically different claim — that cycle length governs the *reversal speed* of new accruals — and it explains why the flow and stock legs perform similarly despite low correlation. The gate is a bounded rank of a sales-deflated stock, so no denominator instability arises, and the profitability anchor keeps the long leg broad.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OverproductionVsCostBase
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1), GROWTH(cogs, 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: When non-cash current assets grow faster than the cost of goods actually sold, the firm is producing or purchasing ahead of demand — the classic real-earnings-management move that spreads fixed overhead across more units and flatters reported margins while burying the cost in inventory that must later be written down.
considered.reasoning: Every accrual construct in this archive benchmarks working capital against sales or assets; benchmarking against the cost base instead targets the production decision directly, which is the economically correct denominator for inventory and detects margin inflation that a revenue-based benchmark cannot see. It also gives the asset-side decomposition the economic content the critic found missing earlier, since here the asset side is paired with its own cost driver rather than simply deleted from the standard accrual formula.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CredibilityWeightedProfitability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Accruals should not be traded as a signal in their own right but used as a credibility weight on the profitability signal: reported gross profitability deserves to be believed in proportion to how little of it was created by an expanding operating cycle, so a firm's profitability score should be discounted toward neutrality as its accruals rise.
considered.reasoning: Every archive construct either adds the two legs or amplifies the accrual by a state variable; this inverts the architecture by making accruals the multiplier on the quality signal, so that high-accrual firms are pushed toward the middle of the sort rather than to the short leg and the extremes are populated only by profitability that is verifiably cash-backed. That is an economically different claim — accruals govern the *reliability* of the quality measure rather than carrying an independent return premium — and it is falsifiable against the additive baseline on identical, well-covered inputs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OperatingAssetBuildFundedByShortDebt
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at), 1))), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Receivables and inventory that a firm funds by drawing on short-term debt represent an operating cycle that does not pay for itself; the combination of swelling operating assets and rising revolver balances precedes both inventory write-downs and refinancing stress, whereas the same asset build funded internally is ordinary growth.
considered.reasoning: The critic correctly identified that Δdlc appears inside the standard accrual construct, so the gate was partly a transform of the leg it conditioned; restricting the accrual leg to the asset side, Δ(act − che), removes dlc entirely and makes the funding variable a clean, economically exogenous state. The mechanism — who financed the operating cycle — is untested in the archive and distinct from both the static leverage gate and the cash-drain gate, since a firm that borrows short-term can keep its cash balance flat and evade both.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ThreeYearCashBackedProfitGeneration
considered.expression: IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(SUB(revt, cogs), 3), SUB(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 3))), at))
considered.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings are best measured over a full multi-year stretch: the gross profit a firm has cumulatively earned over three years, less the working capital that expansion permanently consumed, is the profit that was actually available to owners rather than recycled into receivables and inventory.
considered.reasoning: The defective cumulative-profit denominator is eliminated — absorption is now expressed as a difference in the numerator with total assets as a uniformly positive deflator — so the sign can no longer flip for the low-profit distressed firms the measure targets. The three-year horizon is the economic point rather than a parameter tweak: it distinguishes firms that generate cash-backed profit through a whole investment cycle from those whose single-year cash conversion is a timing accident, and it restores coverage relative to the five-year version.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AbnormalAccrualBeyondSalesNeed
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1))), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm needs additional working capital in proportion to its revenue expansion at its own established operating-cycle intensity; only the accrual *in excess of* that mechanically required amount reflects discretionary recognition, so subtracting the expected build isolates genuine accounting aggressiveness from ordinary growth financing.
considered.reasoning: The archive has approached this idea only through gates that mute the accrual for growing firms, which discards information rather than adjusting it; here the expected accrual — last year's working-capital intensity multiplied by this year's sales change — is explicitly subtracted, producing a residual that stays informative for high-growth and low-growth firms alike. This is the natural sharpening of the mechanism behind the archive's best signal, and it deflates by assets with a firm-specific expectation model rather than a rank gate, so it should raise the cross-sectional slope and the long-leg quality simultaneously.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildDuringProfitDecline
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Managers reach for accounting flexibility precisely when the underlying business is deteriorating, so a working-capital build coinciding with falling profitability is the signature of an attempt to mask decline, whereas the same build at a firm with improving profitability reflects an expanding, healthy operating base.
considered.reasoning: Profitability *change* has been tested only as an additive leg, where it delivered a weak 2.9% alpha because it discarded the profitability anchor; as a conditioning state it plays a different role, identifying the population in which accrual manipulation has motive. It is economically distinct from the demand gate — a firm can grow revenue while its margins collapse, which is exactly the discount-and-stuff pattern this gate targets and the sales-growth gate misses.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AbnormalAccrualConservatismStreak
considered.expression: SUMRANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), MUL(RATIO(LAG(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), LAG(sale, 1)), DELTA(sale, 1)))), 0), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Reporting conservatism is a durable managerial regime rather than an annual outcome, and the cleanest evidence of it is a repeated record of working-capital builds falling short of what revenue growth would have justified; five years of such restraint identifies management that does not use the operating cycle to manufacture reported performance.
